title: Utility Types
subtitle: Partial, Required, Readonly, Pick, Omit, Record, ReturnType — TypeScript's built-in type transformers
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: You often need variations of an existing type: a version where all fields are optional (for updates), a version where certain fields are excluded (for a public API response), or a readonly version (for configuration). Rewriting the type by hand leads to duplication.
whyItExists.solution: TypeScript ships built-in utility types — generic type transformers that derive a new type from an existing one. Partial<T> makes all fields optional. Pick<T, K> keeps only certain fields. Omit<T, K> removes certain fields.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Whenever you need a modified version of an existing type. These are everyday tools in TypeScript — use them liberally.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Don't chain multiple utility types when the result would be confusing. If you need a very specific shape, just write it as a new interface. Utility types are for common transformations, not every case.

explainModes.beginner: Imagine you have a User type with 10 fields. When you update a user, you might only change 2 or 3 fields. Instead of writing a new UpdateUser type with all those fields as optional, you write Partial<User> — it automatically makes every field optional. These are shortcuts for common type patterns.
explainModes.simple: Partial<T> — all fields optional. Required<T> — all fields required (removes ?). Readonly<T> — all fields readonly. Pick<T, 'a' | 'b'> — keep only those fields. Omit<T, 'a' | 'b'> — remove those fields. Record<K, V> — object type with keys of type K and values of type V. ReturnType<typeof fn> — the return type of a function. Parameters<typeof fn> — tuple of parameter types.
explainModes.standard: These are implemented with mapped types and conditional types in the TS standard library. Partial<T> = { [K in keyof T]?: T[K] }. Required<T> = { [K in keyof T]-?: T[K] } (the - removes ?). Readonly<T> = { readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] }. Pick<T, K> = { [P in K]: T[P] }. Omit<T, K> = Pick<T, Exclude<keyof T, K>>. NonNullable<T> removes null and undefined from a union.
explainModes.technical: Awaited<T> — unwraps Promises: Awaited<Promise<string>> = string. ConstructorParameters<T> — parameter tuple of a class constructor. InstanceType<T> — instance type of a class. ThisType<T> — sets the this type inside an object literal. Mutable<T> (community pattern) — removes readonly: { -readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] }. DeepPartial<T> — recursive partial (not built-in, but commonly implemented).
explainModes.deepDive: The utility types are implemented in lib.es5.d.ts using template literal types, mapped types, and conditional types. You can implement your own: type DeepReadonly<T> = { readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] extends object ? DeepReadonly<T[K]> : T[K] }. Template literal utility types: Uppercase<S>, Lowercase<S>, Capitalize<S>, Uncapitalize<S> — transform string literal types. type Keys<T> = keyof T extends string ? Uppercase<keyof T> : never.

questions.question: You have `interface User { id: number; name: string; password: string }`. Which utility type gives you a new type with all fields except password?
options: Both Pick and Omit work — pick the one you prefer
questions.explanation: Both work! Pick<User, 'id' | 'name'> keeps only the listed fields. Omit<User, 'password'> removes the listed field and keeps the rest. For large interfaces, Omit is more convenient (fewer fields to list). For small interfaces or when you want explicit control over what's exposed, Pick is clearer. Real code uses both.

faq.q: Is there a built-in DeepPartial utility type?
faq.a: No, but it's commonly implemented: type DeepPartial<T> = T extends object ? { [K in keyof T]?: DeepPartial<T[K]> } : T. TypeScript doesn't include it because recursive mapped types have some edge cases. Libraries like 'utility-types' or 'ts-essentials' provide DeepPartial and other recursive variants.

examples: function updateUser(id: number, data: Partial<User>): Promise<User>
type ApiResponse<T> = Readonly<{ data: T; status: number }>
